methodology_lines: Each Scope 3 category is calculated by one of the methods below, and every export names the method used for each category in that inventory. For Categories 1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 9, 10, 11, 13, 14 and 15, a figure entered directly is used instead of any estimate. Categories 5, 6, 7 and 12 take no entered figure: they are calculated only from the data their method asks for.

Categories 1, 2 and 4 (purchased goods and services; capital goods; upstream transportation and distribution): Spend-based, priced from EXIOBASE 3 version 3.8.2 (EXIOBASE consortium, licensed CC BY-SA 4.0) through the active factor edition, using the factor recorded for that category (an EXIOBASE industry or product, whichever the category is priced against) in the EXIOBASE region the inventory's country of supply belongs to. For Category 1, supplier-specific figures, where entered, are used instead.

Category 5 (waste generated in operations): Activity-based: tonnes of waste by material and treatment route, each multiplied by the kg CO2e per tonne published for that pair in UK DEFRA/DESNZ (2026) GHG Conversion Factors for Company Reporting (full set v1, Waste disposal sheet, AR5 GWPs). Only the routes published for a material are offered; re-use is not a disposal route and has no factor. Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

Category 12 (end-of-life treatment of sold products): Activity-based, per material: the tonnes of sold products and packaging reaching end of life, split by the customer across the treatment routes the sheet publishes for that material, each route's tonnes multiplied by the kg CO2e per tonne published for that material and route in UK DEFRA/DESNZ (2026) GHG Conversion Factors for Company Reporting (full set v1, Waste disposal sheet, AR5 GWPs). This is finer than formula [12.1] of the GHG Protocol's Technical Guidance for Calculating Scope 3 Emissions, which applies one average factor per treatment method. The split and its source are the customer's assumption. The figure is the expected end-of-life emissions of all products sold in the reporting year, most of which have not yet occurred. These are UK factors, applied wherever the products are sold. Re-use is not a treatment route and has no factor. Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

Category 6 (business travel): Activity-based, per flight leg and rail journey: passenger-km (the direct one-way distance times the passengers or trips) multiplied by the kg CO2e per passenger-km published in UK DEFRA/DESNZ (2026) GHG Conversion Factors for Company Reporting (full set v1, Business travel- air and Business travel- land sheets, AR5 GWPs), with well-to-tank emissions from the matching well-to-tank sheets added. Each flight leg takes one of the sheet's categories: domestic when both ends are in the UK; the haul the Haul definition sheet gives the other end when one end is; and, when neither end is, domestic under 482.8032 km, short-haul from 482.8032 km to under 3,701.4912 km and long-haul from 3,701.4912 km, which departs from the sheet's guidance to use its international average for flights between non-UK countries (Business travel- air A56) and follows the distance bands of the US EPA GHG Emission Factors Hub (2025), cited as the precedent for banding only, with no EPA figure used. Radiative forcing is included unless the inventory turns it off, using DEFRA's With RF flight factors, which increase the CO2 component by 70% to account for radiative forcing (Business travel- air A11), and the setting is recorded with each inventory. The sheet's flight factors include a distance uplift of 8% for indirect routing (Business travel- air A49), so each leg's distance is the direct distance with no uplift added. They are for direct (non-stop) flights (Business travel- air A53), so a journey with a stop is entered as one leg per flight. Rail journeys are priced from the sheet's rail factors and their well-to-tank factors, which are UK figures; for a journey outside the UK they are used as a stand-in, and the journey is flagged. Hotel stays are not included: they are optional under the GHG Protocol Scope 3 Standard, and the licence for the published hotel factors has not been confirmed. Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

Category 7 (employee commuting): Activity-based, per group of employees who commute the same way: employees times the one-way distance times 2, times the days commuted per week, times the weeks per year, multiplied by the kg CO2e published in UK DEFRA/DESNZ (2026) GHG Conversion Factors for Company Reporting (full set v1, Business travel- land sheet, AR5 GWPs) with well-to-tank emissions from the matching sheet added. Car and motorbike factors are per vehicle-km and are divided by the occupancy the customer enters; walking and cycling count as zero. These are UK factors. For a group commuting outside the UK they are used as a stand-in, and the row is flagged. Homeworking is optional under the GHG Protocol Scope 3 Standard (p. 46). Where entered, it is priced from the Homeworking sheet’s combined office equipment and heating factor per FTE working hour (Homeworking C24), for employees in the UK only: the factor is a UK average (Homeworking A11), mostly heating, with no cooling component. The workbook does not state whether it counts only the additional energy of working from home, which the GHG Protocol’s Technical Guidance asks for (p. 90). Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

Category 15 (investments): PCAF-aligned financed emissions. A known total, where entered, replaces the holding-level figures. Otherwise each holding's figure is the investee's emissions as entered by the customer, multiplied by the outstanding amount over the value its PCAF asset class attributes on, capped at 100%. Investee emissions are used on whatever GWP basis each investee reported, not re-based, and ThemisIQ does not record which basis that was. A holding missing its emissions, outstanding amount or attribution value withholds the category figure. A portfolio value multiplied by a spend factor does not measure emissions, so ThemisIQ does not estimate this category that way.

Categories 3, 8, 9, 10, 11, 13 and 14 (fuel- and energy-related activities; upstream leased assets; downstream transportation and distribution; processing of sold products; use of sold products; downstream leased assets; franchises): A flat 0.5 kg CO2e per unit of the inventory's currency entered, the same for every category priced this way, whatever the figure represents. This factor is recorded with no published source, no year and no region.
shared.assistant_scope3: Categories 1, 2 and 4 (purchased goods and services; capital goods; upstream transportation and distribution) are priced from EXIOBASE 3.8.2 through a named factor edition, by sector or product and country, and for Category 1 also from supplier-specific figures where the customer enters them; Category 5 (waste generated in operations) is priced from the UK DEFRA/DESNZ 2026 waste factors, per material and treatment route; Category 12 (end-of-life treatment of sold products) is priced from the same UK DEFRA/DESNZ 2026 waste factors, per material and treatment route, applied to the tonnes of sold products reaching end of life as the customer splits them across routes; Category 6 (business travel) is priced from the UK DEFRA/DESNZ 2026 business travel factors, per flight leg (by origin, destination, cabin class and distance) and per rail journey, with well-to-tank emissions added, radiative forcing included unless the inventory turns it off, and hotel stays not included; Category 7 (employee commuting) is priced from the UK DEFRA/DESNZ 2026 land travel factors, per group of employees by mode, distance, days commuted and, for cars and motorbikes, occupancy, with well-to-tank emissions added, and homeworking priced only for employees in the UK; Category 15 (investments) is assessed through a PCAF-aligned path; and Categories 3, 8, 9, 10, 11, 13 and 14 (fuel- and energy-related activities; upstream leased assets; downstream transportation and distribution; processing of sold products; use of sold products; downstream leased assets; franchises) are priced from ONE flat factor of 0.5 kg CO2e per unit of the inventory's currency, the same for every category priced this way, whatever the figure represents, with no source, year or region recorded. Those seven are a rough order-of-magnitude estimate, not a sourced figure, and every export names the method used for each category
shared.assistant_gwp: In the Scope 3 module, Categories 5 and 12 use the UK DEFRA/DESNZ 2026 waste factors, which their publisher combined on AR5; Category 6 uses the UK DEFRA/DESNZ 2026 business travel factors, which their publisher combined on AR5; Category 7 uses the UK DEFRA/DESNZ 2026 land travel and homeworking factors, which their publisher combined on AR5; Category 15 uses investee emissions on whatever GWP basis each investee reported, not re-based, and ThemisIQ does not record which basis that was.

Method, in the GHG Protocol Scope 3 Standard's terms for Category 5: waste-type-specific for row 1, where a specific material was chosen; average-data for row 2, because Household residual waste is an unsorted residual stream of unknown composition.

GWP basis: AR5. Stated by the workbook's Introduction sheet: the CO2e figures use IPCC Fifth Assessment Report (AR5) 100-year GWPs. The values are combined CO2e as published and are not re-based. The linked GHG inventory records AR6. These factors are not re-based to it, so the inventory combines AR6 and AR5 figures.

For landfill, the factors in the tables include collection, transportation and landfill emissions (‘gate to grave’). For combustion and recycling, the factors consider transport to an energy recovery or materials reclamation facility only. This is in line with GHG Protocol Guidelines, with subsequent emissions attributed to electricity generation or recycled material production respectively.

These factors cannot be used to determine the relative lifecycle merit of different waste management options. This is because the emissions from energy recovery, recycling, composting and anaerobic digestion are attributed to the user of the recycled materials, not the producer of the waste, in line with GHG Protocol Guidelines.
Each material is offered only the treatment routes the sheet publishes a factor for. A route it does not publish is not offered, and is not treated as zero.

Re-use is not offered. The workbook's FAQ, "Why there are no conversion factors for the disposal method "Re-use"?": "Re-use" is not within the scope of the GHG conversion factors because it is not a waste disposal method. Only the disposal of waste at the end of its life is within scope.
The sheet publishes no wastewater factors, so wastewater treatment is not in this figure.

For each group of employees who commute the same way, the distance is the one-way distance times 2 for the return trip, times the days commuted per week, times the weeks per year, times the employees in the group; each mode’s factor is applied to that distance, and walking and cycling are counted at zero.

Commuting days are as entered by the customer: the days per week actually commuted, times the weeks per year, excluding homeworking, holiday and business-travel days, as the GHG Protocol’s Technical Guidance describes (p. 92).

Car and motorbike factors are per vehicle-km, the whole vehicle (Business travel- land A12), so each group’s distance is divided by the occupancy the customer entered for it, which may be an average such as 1.3 from an occupancy survey. These are UK factors. For a group commuting outside the UK they are used as a stand-in, and the row is flagged.

For combustion and recycling, the factors consider transport to an energy recovery or materials reclamation facility only. This is in line with GHG Protocol Guidelines, with subsequent emissions attributed to electricity generation or recycled material production respectively.

These factors cannot be used to determine the relative lifecycle merit of different waste management options. This is because the emissions from energy recovery, recycling, composting and anaerobic digestion are attributed to the user of the recycled materials, not the producer of the waste, in line with GHG Protocol Guidelines.

Re-use is not offered as a route: a re-used product still reaches end of life later. The workbook's FAQ, "Why there are no conversion factors for the disposal method "Re-use"?": "Re-use" is not within the scope of the GHG conversion factors because it is not a waste disposal method. Only the disposal of waste at the end of its life is within scope.
UK DEFRA/DESNZ (2026) GHG Conversion Factors for Company Reporting, Waste disposal sheet, per material and route, on the customer's split

Activity-based, per material: the tonnes of sold products and packaging reaching end of life, split by the customer across the treatment routes the sheet publishes for that material, each route's tonnes multiplied by the kg CO2e per tonne published for that material and route in UK DEFRA/DESNZ (2026) GHG Conversion Factors for Company Reporting (full set v1, Waste disposal sheet, AR5 GWPs). This is finer than formula [12.1] of the GHG Protocol's Technical Guidance for Calculating Scope 3 Emissions, which applies one average factor per treatment method. The split and its source are the customer's assumption. The figure is the expected end-of-life emissions of all products sold in the reporting year, most of which have not yet occurred. These are UK factors, applied wherever the products are sold. Re-use is not a treatment route and has no factor. cat15.guidance: Emissions associated with your investments and lending (financed emissions), for investors, banks and asset owners. ThemisIQ assesses this holding by holding on PCAF’s method: each investee’s emissions as entered by the customer, multiplied by your share of that investee. A portfolio value multiplied by a spend factor does not measure emissions, so ThemisIQ does not estimate this category that way. ThemisIQ is not PCAF-certified or a PCAF signatory.
